headline_marked: Apple Music to [[Open New Concert Venue]] in London's Battersea Power Station
headline: Apple Music to Open New Concert Venue in London's Battersea Power Station
summary: The 600-capacity venue will host live shows, filmed and broadcast online, featuring state-of-the-art tech with more cameras and speakers than any venue of its size globally.
details: Apple is launching a new concert venue, dubbed Apple Music Hall, beneath its European headquarters at London's Battersea Power Station. The 600-capacity space is designed to host live performances by major artists and emerging bands, with all shows being filmed and broadcast live on Apple Music.

The venue boasts advanced technology, including more cameras and speakers than any other venue of its size worldwide, according to Apple Music's vice president, Oliver Schusser. This initiative aims to create bespoke content that distinguishes Apple Music from competitors like Spotify and Amazon Music.

Apple Music Hall is equipped with a 38-foot stage that can be configured for various performance styles, along with specialized dressing rooms. The facility also includes new studios for Apple Music's radio stations, DJ mixes, writing camps, and band rehearsals, enabling artists to record podcasts, appear on radio shows, and live-stream gigs all in the same day.

The move reflects a broader strategy to foster deeper connections between artists and fans, addressing concerns that current music streaming services are "one dimensional." Apple aims to provide artists with more avenues to connect with their audience beyond just playlisting.

This venture marks Apple's return to hosting live music events in London, nine years after the discontinuation of the popular iTunes Festival. The company hopes to support new and upcoming bands who may struggle to gain traction in the current music landscape.

headline_marked: [[AI-generated writing is unreadable]] and impersonal, experts say
headline: AI-generated writing is unreadable and impersonal, experts say
summary: Developers are increasingly fed up with AI-generated content, finding it lacks context, perspective, and humanity. A new survey reveals most readers stop engaging with AI-assisted articles.
details: The rise of AI tools has led to an explosion of AI-generated content, from design proposals and business plans to code documentation and blog posts. While AI can assist in writing, many find the output to be 'unreadable' and 'inhumane' due to a lack of context and perspective.

A significant frustration is the use of AI to retrospectively summarize existing work into design documents. These summaries, while detailed, fail to serve their original purpose of building consensus or refining ideas through human thought.

Pull request summaries, tickets, and meeting notes are also increasingly machine-generated, leading to a loss of crucial context. Questions about the 'why,' 'value,' and 'urgency' of work are left unanswered, making it difficult for human collaborators to engage effectively.

Even personal communications are being AI-assisted, resulting in messages that are impersonal, dispassionate, and disjointed. The author argues that authentic human expression, even with its flaws, is far more valuable than a polished but soulless AI rewrite.

A recent survey highlights this sentiment, with 78% of developers reporting they stop reading articles they suspect are AI-assisted. Furthermore, 71% avoid authors who use AI extensively, preferring genuine human writing with its unique voice and idiosyncrasies.

The core issue is that AI-generated text often lacks the 'author's voice' that Bjarne Stroustrup, creator of C++, values in books. This authentic voice, complete with peculiarities, creates a connection that dry, academic, or machine-generated text cannot replicate.
